historical_timeline.summary: Born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia; raised in Baltimore.
Her mother died; her drinking and drug use increased.
Arrested for narcotics possession; sentenced to a year and a day.
Released early from federal custody; lost her New York cabaret card.
Drinking increased over the following seven years.
Died at Metropolitan Hospital in New York.

claims.statement: Billie Holiday was born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia on April 7, 1915, and was raised in Baltimore by her mother, Sarah Julia "Sadie" Fagan.
Her mother died in October 1945; afterwards Holiday drank more heavily and her drug use increased as she grieved.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic alcohol use disorder. The cause of her mother's death is not given in the cited sources.

source_links.locator: addiction severe after her mother's death

claims.statement: Holiday began using heroin in the early 1940s, and her addiction became severe in the late 1940s; she was arrested repeatedly over her heroin use in that period.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic opioid use disorder. The arrests are recorded as part of her history, without judgment.

source_links.locator: became addicted to heroin during 1943 and 1944

claims.statement: In May 1947 Holiday was arrested for narcotics possession; she pleaded guilty, was sentenced to a year and a day, and was held at the federal facility for women at Alderson, West Virginia, until her early release on March 16, 1948.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Release after a long period of enforced abstinence carries a high risk of overdose; the modern episode begins five weeks after her release. One source names the place as "Alderston, Virginia," an evident error.

claims.statement: Holiday sought treatment for her addiction, at one point checking herself into an institution in the hope of breaking her habit.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports her own wish to recover, which the episode builds on. The source gives no date.

claims.statement: Her conviction cost her the New York City cabaret card she needed to perform in clubs that served alcohol.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A loss of income and work tied to the conviction; part of her social history.

source_links.locator: denied a license to perform in establishments that sold alcohol

claims.statement: The Federal Bureau of Narcotics pursued Holiday for years, and later writers have described that pursuit as driven by racism and linked it to her performance of "Strange Fruit," a song against lynching.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation by later writers; recorded to support trauma-informed care, and not used to state any person's motives as fact.

claims.statement: Her autobiography, Lady Sings the Blues, written in collaboration with William Dufty, was published in 1956.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; not quoted in the record.

claims.statement: In 1959 Holiday was admitted to Metropolitan Hospital in New York with liver and heart problems and was diagnosed with cirrhosis. While she was in the hospital she was arrested for narcotics possession and kept under police guard. She died there on July 17, 1959, aged 44; the cause of death is given as cirrhosis of the liver with pulmonary edema, or pulmonary edema and heart failure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode, recorded as a fact without detail. The episode records no liver diagnosis. One source dates her death to July 15, 1959.

source_links.locator: admitted to the hospital for heart and liver problems

claims.statement: After 1950 she slipped deeper into alcohol use over the following seven years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; supports the decision to treat her alcohol use from the start of the episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evidence-based, non-stigmatizing, trauma-informed primary care for a 33-year-old singer with a severe opioid use disorder and a moderate alcohol use disorder, five weeks after release from custody, when overdose risk is highest: starting buprenorphine in primary care, naloxone and overdose education, acamprosate for alcohol because naltrexone cannot be combined with buprenorphine, PEth to follow drinking, hepatitis, HIV, and liver screening with FIB-4 fibrosis staging, hepatitis A and B vaccination, depression screening with a structured safety assessment and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and an integrated recovery plan that continues medication through a return to use rather than requiring linear recovery, on the ASAM, SAMHSA, VA/DoD, and AASLD guidance and the CMID depression monograph.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Holiday returns one week after starting buprenorphine with naloxone and is seen by Dr. Ortiz of addiction medicine on the same day. She took half a film on the first day and one film daily since, under the tongue each morning, without missing a dose. She has used no heroin or other opioids. She had no withdrawal, but cravings come back each evening, most of all after a show. She has had mild constipation and no drowsiness. She picked up two naloxone two-packs; her friend came with her and was shown how to use them. She is still drinking four or five drinks on performance nights. She read her results from last week by phone. She says she came back because nobody lectured her at the first visit.

consultant_note.history: Ms. Holiday, a 33-year-old singer, is seen at the request of Dr. Mayfield one week after starting buprenorphine with naloxone. She has taken every dose, 4 mg on the first day and 8 mg since, and has used no opioids. She has had no withdrawal, but cravings return each evening, especially after shows. She drinks four or five drinks on performance nights to calm her nerves. She has no history of withdrawal seizures or delirium. She sought treatment for heroin use years ago and says she wants to stay off it and keep singing. Her biggest fear is overdosing now that her tolerance is low. She tours often and worries about getting prescriptions filled on the road. She asked that this note be shared only with Dr. Mayfield
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Mayfield's intake note with the safety assessment, AUDIT-C, DAST-10, and PHQ-9. Last week's results: AST 52, ALT 38, GGT 84 U/L; albumin 4.0 g/dL; bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL; MCV 101 fL; platelets 236; creatinine 0.72 mg/dL; PEth 312 ng/mL; hepatitis C antibody nonreactive (0.09); hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody nonreactive, surface antibody 3 mIU/mL; HIV antigen-antibody nonreactive. Today's urine drug test: buprenorphine and norbuprenorphine only. Prescription drug monitoring program: no other controlled-substance prescriptions

assessment.assessment: Buprenorphine is a good choice: it lowers the risk of overdose death, can be prescribed from primary care, and fits her touring better than daily methadone clinic attendance, which remains an option if buprenorphine does not control her cravings. Extended-release naltrexone would need a long opioid-free period and does not protect her if she loses tolerance and uses again. Starting at a low dose was right after enforced abstinence. Evening cravings at 8 mg mean the dose is too low; most people do best at 16 mg or more

Naltrexone, the usual first choice, cannot be used with buprenorphine. Acamprosate is safe with buprenorphine and with her normal kidney function; topiramate is a second choice. Her withdrawal risk is low, so she does not need a medically managed withdrawal

AST higher than ALT with a raised GGT and a high MCV points to alcohol. Albumin, bilirubin, and platelets are normal, and FIB-4 is 1.18, below 1.3, so advanced fibrosis is unlikely and elastography is not needed now. Repeating liver tests as drinking changes, and FIB-4 within a year, is enough. She is not immune to hepatitis B and should complete the series
A return to use is common and is a reason to strengthen treatment, not to stop it. Her greatest risk is a gap in her medication while touring

recommendations: Increase buprenorphine with naloxone to 16 mg once daily today
Start acamprosate 666 mg three times daily; continue thiamine while she drinks heavily
Naloxone at home and in her bag, with her friend trained; fentanyl test strips; never use alone
Visits every one to two weeks for the first month, then every two to four weeks until stable, then monthly; telehealth check-ins when she is on tour
Urine drug testing with fentanyl at most visits early on, explained as part of care, never as a condition of treatment; check the prescription drug monitoring program before each prescription
PEth with liver tests at each check while she is drinking; FIB-4 again at six to twelve months; elastography only if FIB-4 reaches 1.3
Complete the hepatitis A and B vaccine series; repeat hepatitis C and HIV testing yearly while any drug use continues
If she returns to use, keep her on buprenorphine, increase support, and look for the cause; consider monthly extended-release buprenorphine if gaps in supply recur
Plan for tours before each trip: a pharmacy chain that can fill in any state, prior authorization kept current, an early fill, and a travel letter
Offer counseling and peer recovery support without making them a condition of medication
